# Outline — how many benchmarks must be run, which ones, and when does it hold

*Rev. 10, by story-repo (see the revision log). Built from the `Brief` (idea-repo, rev. 10) and the pre-registration (`experiment-repo` `prereg/PREREG.md`, commit 7731e49) and the objective (`story-repo`#1). It says what to test and which figure carries which claim; it never says what a result must be. Each claim has a branch for the case it fails — a failing claim is reported as a finding, not repaired.*

## 0. Working title and scope line
"How many benchmarks must you run? Choosing and sizing the run set that predicts a new model's other scores — evidence from embedding-model leaderboards".
The scope line (title/abstract) names the data the claim is about: **MTEB embedding models**, with the realised M × N stated. "LLM"/"language model" appears in the title only if a generative-LLM matrix with N ≳ 20 supports a claim of its own (Gate G2 below). **G2 is met** by the Open LLM Leaderboard per-subtask matrix (M = 4,507 models × N = 39 subtasks, dense, one harness, fine-tunes/merges of open weights; `story-repo`#7), so the paper's scope is two matrices — MTEB embedding models and open-weight generative LLMs — and "LLM" may enter the title only if the claims it makes are supported on that matrix (decided from its results, not before). The small matrices (Open LLM LB N=6, HELM Lite N=10) stay labelled oracle checks with k ≤ N−1.

## 1. The story in six sentences (the abstract's skeleton)
1. Evaluating a model on every benchmark is costly, and leaderboards hold a model × benchmark matrix with holes; an evaluator can afford only k benchmarks for a new model.
2. The problem is cold-start elicitation (new user, k ratings) and multidimensional adaptive testing; the machinery (probabilistic factor model, A/D/V-optimal greedy design) is classical, and we do not claim a new selection method.
3. What is missing for benchmarks is the answer under the protocol that matches the use: whole new models (grouped by org/family) held out, selection and fitting on other models only, error scored on a common target set of benchmarks that no selector can choose (the score on the cells left unrun is kept as a secondary).
4. We give a closed-form risk for the factor model (floor + design term + residual) that attributes the error, and test on synthetic data (known truth) and on the real matrix whether a sufficiency rule k*(ε) read off the spectrum carries; on real data it does not; on the primary (common-target) score the design term is predicted well (T1 is conservative for it), but the floor term, which dominates from k ≈ 8, is about 2.5× what the factor model predicts, and the cause of that misfit is not identified (Brief rev. 10); T1 is a decomposition of the design part, not a predictor of the floor.
5. Main result (numbers from the common-target-set rerun): the error-vs-k curve on held-out groups; the k that gets within ε points of the floor, for a range of ε; designed selection matters when k is very small (≤ 5) and random-k is within noise from about k = 8 at the coarse scale; beyond that the error sits in the floor, which is larger than the factor model predicts; that better inference rather than better selection would lower it is a hypothesis, carried as a claim only if Table 3 shows an inference rule lowering the excess over the floor by more than δ_floor (part of the residual may be the floor itself), and no k resolves neighbouring models (floor ≈ 5 points on the common target set; the pre-set margin of about 0.1 point, set by adjacent-model gaps, is not reached at any k).
6. Scope map: where the answer holds and where it never reaches the floor (extrapolation to new families/strongest models, sparse coverage, small M, saturation, granularity).

9:## What the contribution is (and is not)
10:The machinery is classical: item selection by A-/D-optimal design for a latent trait vector (multidimensional computerized adaptive testing, Mulder & van der Linden 2009), cold-start active learning for matrix factorisation (Rashid 2002, Golbandi 2011, Houlsby 2014), probabilistic PCA, greedy subset selection with submodularity-ratio guarantees. **I do not claim a new selection method.** The contribution is: (i) the empirical answer on real leaderboard matrices under the protocol that matches the use (whole new models held out, by group; selection fit on others only); (ii) the **empirical needed-k curve** k*(ε) (excess over the all-others floor, with group-bootstrap CI), an **error decomposition** (residual floor + design term + misfit) that attributes where the error sits at each k, and a test of whether a spectrum-based rule predicts k* (interim result: it does not; see "Interim results" below; the failure and its cause are part of the contribution); (iii) the **scope map**: where the answer holds and where it never reaches the floor (extrapolation to new families/strongest models, sparse coverage, small M, saturated scores, task granularity), including a misspecification ladder on synthetic data on which real matrices are placed.
58:1. *T1 as a decomposition, not a rule.* At k=20, MSE 44.8 = floor/noise 30.6 + noise misfit 1.0 + design 2.1 + residual (estimation + misspecification) 11.0 [7.9, 14.1]. The design term is small and correctly sized; the misfit term is not small and is what a spectrum-based rule misses. The paper therefore states: the closed-form risk **attributes** the error and explains the shape of the gain from design (large at k ≤ 5, small after), but a spectrum-and-noise rule for k* does **not** carry on real data. The empirical k*(ε) curve is the answer. Contribution and abstract are worded this way; no "k from the spectrum" claim.
59:2. *Why (to be shown, not asserted).* The 11.0 term is a residual: it mixes finite-M estimation error (T1's ~1/M term) with misspecification, and the paper calls it "residual (estimation + misspecification)" until separated. The separation comes from known-truth synthetic runs at the same M (training size) and k: the estimation share is what those runs give, and only the remainder is attributed to misspecification. Choosing the first two or three benchmarks by the factor model's design criterion is clearly better than choosing them at random (about 1.9 points of RMSE on the target benchmarks). From about eight benchmarks on, random selection is practically as good, within a quarter of the floor, and what is left is the floor: about 8 benchmarks bring a new model within 2 points of what all of its other scores predict, 32 to 50 within 1 point, and no number we tried resolves neighbouring models. These numbers are for held-out organisations on this matrix, with the margins stated in Section~\ref{sec:protocol}; the scope experiments say how they move, in units of the floor, when the data are thinner.

\paragraph{Limits.}
The run sets are not random: a model's observed cells are the tasks its authors chose to run, which may differ from the tasks a new model's evaluator can run, and the target scores are single measurements. The temporal and strength splits rest on 13 and 22 models from 4 and 11 organisations, so what they say about extrapolation is indicative. The factor model is linear in the latent factors; the real matrix is outside every single misspecification we tried, and the cause of the factor $2.5$ between the measured and predicted floor is not identified, so the paper does not claim that a better inference rule, rather than a better run set, would lower the error. The adaptive and kernel baselines are our adaptations of methods from other settings, and the greedy rule is not exhaustive. The results are for embedding models on MTEB and make no statement about other kinds of model.

\label{sec:release}
The derived matrix, the code that produces every number, table and figure, the result files and notes for reproducing them are released with the paper. The raw scores are the public MTEB results repository (CC0-1.0) at commit \texttt{6dabbcc68c28ea5f180ce7df79347b3ca9cc6383}.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Leaderboards hold a matrix of models by benchmarks with many holes: most models were run on a few of the benchmarks, and an evaluator with a new model can afford to run only $k$ of the $N$. Three questions follow. Which $k$ benchmarks should be run? How should the model's scores on the others be inferred from them and from the historical matrix? And how large must $k$ be before the answer is good enough? The first two are the cold-start problem of recommender systems and item selection in adaptive testing, whose machinery (a probabilistic factor model, a greedy optimal-design criterion) is classical, and we do not claim a new selection method. What is missing for benchmarks is the answer to the third question under the protocol that matches the use: whole new models, grouped by the organisation that made them, are held out, everything is fitted on the other models, and the error is measured on benchmarks that no selection rule could have chosen.

That last condition matters. If each rule is scored on the benchmarks it leaves unrun, rules that run the hardest benchmarks remove them from their own targets and can score below the error of predicting from all the other benchmarks, and the target changes with $k$. We therefore split the benchmarks at random into a pool from which a rule may choose and a target set it may not, repeat this over 50 splits, and report the excess over each model's own error when all of the pool is given, its floor (Section~\ref{sec:protocol}). \section{Related work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Cheaper evaluation within one benchmark.}
tinyBenchmarks~\citep{polo2024tinybenchmarks}, metabench~\citep{kipnis2024metabench} and anchor points~\citep{vivek2024anchor} choose \emph{examples} of one benchmark so that its full score can be recovered. We choose \emph{whole benchmarks} and predict \emph{other} benchmarks, so the target is not a function of what was run; their latent-ability estimators are the nearest machinery to our inference model.

\paragraph{Low-dimensional structure of model scores.}
Observational scaling laws~\citep{ruan2024observational} and Sloth~\citep{polo2024sloth} find that scores of language models lie near a low-dimensional capability space and use it to extrapolate across models and families; neither asks which $k$ benchmarks to run for a new model or how large $k$ must be. Agreement between benchmarks depends on analysis choices~\citep{perlitz2024benchbench}, which is why our protocol fixes the matrix definition and the margins before any result (Section~\ref{sec:protocol}).

\paragraph{Cold-start elicitation, matrix completion and factor models.}
Which items to ask a new user to rate is the cold-start problem of recommenders~\citep{rashid2002getting,golbandi2011adaptive,elahi2016survey,houlsby2014coldstart}; a new model is a new user, a benchmark an item. Probabilistic PCA with missing data~\citep{tipping1999ppca} supplies our inference model. Matrix-completion theory~\citep{candes2009exact,candes2010power,mazumder2010spectral} assumes the observed entries are sampled at random, whereas here the new row's observed set is \emph{chosen}.

\paragraph{Optimal design and adaptive testing.}
Choosing columns to predict the rest is column subset selection~\citep{boutsidis2009css}; greedy selection carries guarantees through the submodularity ratio~\citep{das2011submodular,bian2017guarantees} and Bayesian experimental design~\citep{chaloner1995bayesian}, and multidimensional adaptive testing selects items by such criteria to measure a latent ability vector~\citep{mulder2009multidimensional}. We claim no new selection method; we add the answer for real leaderboard matrices with missing cells and whole models held out, the measured curve of how many benchmarks are needed, a decomposition of the error, and the conditions under which the answer holds.
E
